e-8256.knowledge_point: Calculating the Derivative of a Multivariable Function With One Independent Variable
e-8256.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14059013/assets/f01b253f560405a8c0f4be8f8797c652fb0ddf774f4db110b8822313b8ac50f3.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $t,$ where $x = x(t)$ and $y=y(t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}t} 
= \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=-y\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy),\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-x\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =-{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t{e}^{t}), \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-t\operatorname{sin}⁡(t{e}^{t}).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=1,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}={e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} \\  & =[-{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t{e}^{t})]\cdot 1+[-t\operatorname{sin}⁡(t{e}^{t})]\cdot {e}^{t} \\  & =-{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t{e}^{t})-t{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t{e}^{t}) \\  & =-(1+t){e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t{e}^{t}).\end{aligned}
$$

e-8257.knowledge_point: Calculating the Derivative of a Multivariable Function With One Independent Variable in the Special Case
e-8257.worked_solution:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y = y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{x+y}},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{x+y}}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\sqrt{x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x}} \\  & =\frac{1-\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\sqrt{x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

e-8258.knowledge_point: Calculating the Derivative of a Multivariable Function With Two Independent Variables
e-8258.problem: Let $f(x,y) = x^2 + y^2,$ where $x = s\cos{t}$ and $y = t\sin{s}.$ Calculate $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial t}.$
e-8258.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14059013/assets/118759b163a4410f66d5855d7b7b1fd9c2ee4be585e778a759997036bd95f765.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t)$ and $y = y(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial t} = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}\cdot \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial t} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}\cdot \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2y\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2s\operatorname{cos}⁡t, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =2t\operatorname{sin}⁡s.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂t} & =-s\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂t} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡s.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂t} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t} \\  & =(2s\operatorname{cos}⁡t)(-s\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+(2t\operatorname{sin}⁡s)(\operatorname{sin}⁡s) \\  & =-2{s}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2t{sin}^{2}⁡s \\  & =2t{sin}^{2}⁡s-2{s}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =2t{sin}^{2}⁡s-{s}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that we used the identity $\sin 2t = 2\sin t\cos t$ in the above simplification.

e-8259.knowledge_point: Calculating the Derivative of a Function of Three Intermediate Variables and Two Independent Variables
e-8259.problem: Let $f(x,y,z) = e^{xy + z},$ where $x = s + t,$ $y = s-t$ and $z = -s^2.$ Calculate $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial t}.$
e-8259.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14059013/assets/b593a1b60fe8c1aef2c5c229ff426db350e6296b9ecb767494283f0fa3342072.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y,z)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t), y = y(s,t)$ and $z = z(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial t} = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}\cdot \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial t} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}\cdot \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial t} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial z}\cdot \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial t}.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x, y$ and $z\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=y{e}^{xy+z},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x{e}^{xy+z},\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}={e}^{xy+z}.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =(s-t){e}^{(s+t)(s-t)-{s}^{2}}=(s-t){e}^{-{t}^{2}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =(s+t){e}^{(s+t)(s-t)-{s}^{2}}=(s+t){e}^{-{t}^{2}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & ={e}^{(s+t)(s-t)-{s}^{2}}={e}^{-{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂t} & =1, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂t} & =-1, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂t} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂t} & =(s-t){e}^{-{t}^{2}}\cdot 1+(s+t){e}^{-{t}^{2}}\cdot (-1)+{e}^{-{t}^{2}}\cdot 0 \\  & =(s-t-s-t){e}^{-{t}^{2}} \\  & =-2t{e}^{-{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14059013/assets/7e5b5001794ecdf2c9b9e9102f334a63d2c59bc6f7511c2eb7fa358fc94cb0c5.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $s,$ where $x=x(s)$ and $y=y(s),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\operatorname{ln}⁡y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=1+\frac{x}{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡2s, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =1+\frac{s}{2s}=\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}=1,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}=2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡2s\cdot 1+\frac{3}{2}\cdot 2 \\  & =3+\operatorname{ln}⁡2s.\end{aligned}
$$

after.html:
Question 1
?

If f(x,y)=y+xln⁡y,x=s and y=2s, compute dfds.

a
32+ln⁡2s
b
34+ln⁡2s
c
ln⁡2s
d
3ln⁡2s
e
3+ln⁡2s
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y) with one independent variable s, where x=x(s) and y=y(s), can be expressed as follows:

dfds=∂f∂x⋅dxds+∂f∂y⋅dyds

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y:

∂f∂x=ln⁡y,∂f∂y=1+xy

Writing the above results in terms of s, we get

∂f∂x=ln⁡2s,∂f∂y=1+s2s=32.

Next, we take the derivatives of x and y with respect to s, and we get

dxds=1,dyds=2.

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

dfds=∂f∂x⋅dxds+∂f∂y⋅dyds=ln⁡2s⋅1+32⋅2=3+ln⁡2s.

content.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14059013/assets/7e5b5001794ecdf2c9b9e9102f334a63d2c59bc6f7511c2eb7fa358fc94cb0c5.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $s,$ where $x=x(s)$ and $y=y(s),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\operatorname{ln}⁡y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=1+\frac{x}{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡2s, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =1+\frac{s}{2s}=\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}=1,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}=2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡2s\cdot 1+\frac{3}{2}\cdot 2 \\  & =3+\operatorname{ln}⁡2s.\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14059013/assets/f01b253f560405a8c0f4be8f8797c652fb0ddf774f4db110b8822313b8ac50f3.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $t,$ where $x=x(t)$ and $y=y(t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡({t}^{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(t), \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡({t}^{2})\operatorname{sin}⁡(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=2t,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡({t}^{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\cdot 2t+(-\operatorname{sin}⁡({t}^{2})\operatorname{sin}⁡(t))\cdot 1 \\  & =2t\operatorname{cos}⁡({t}^{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡({t}^{2})\operatorname{sin}⁡(t).\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14059013/assets/f01b253f560405a8c0f4be8f8797c652fb0ddf774f4db110b8822313b8ac50f3.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $t,$ where $x=x(t)$ and $y=y(t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡({t}^{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(t), \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡({t}^{2})\operatorname{sin}⁡(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=2t,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡({t}^{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\cdot 2t+(-\operatorname{sin}⁡({t}^{2})\operatorname{sin}⁡(t))\cdot 1 \\  & =2t\operatorname{cos}⁡({t}^{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡({t}^{2})\operatorname{sin}⁡(t).\end{aligned}
$$

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $t,$ where $x=x(t)$ and $y=y(t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$

$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-4t\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=4,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot 4+(-4t\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot 1 \\  & =4(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

If f(x,y)=xcos⁡y,x=4t and y=t, compute dfdt.

a
4(sin⁡t−tcos⁡t)
b
4(cos⁡t−tsin⁡t)
c
sin⁡t+4tcos⁡t
d
4(cos⁡t+tsin⁡t)
e
sin⁡t−4tcos⁡t
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y) with one independent variable t, where x=x(t) and y=y(t), can be expressed as follows:

dfdt=∂f∂x⋅dxdt+∂f∂y⋅dydt

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y:

∂f∂x=cos⁡y,∂f∂y=−xsin⁡y

Writing the above results in terms of t, we get

∂f∂x=cos⁡t∂f∂y=−4tsin⁡t.

Next, we take the derivatives of x and y with respect to t, and we get

dxdt=4,dydt=1.

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

dfdt=∂f∂x⋅dxdt+∂f∂y⋅dydt=cos⁡t⋅4+(−4tsin⁡t)⋅1=4(cos⁡t−tsin⁡t).

content.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14059013/assets/f01b253f560405a8c0f4be8f8797c652fb0ddf774f4db110b8822313b8ac50f3.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $t,$ where $x=x(t)$ and $y=y(t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-4t\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=4,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot 4+(-4t\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot 1 \\  & =4(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Substituting gives f(s)=s²/(1+s). The quotient rule yields df/ds=[2s(1+s)−s²]/(1+s)²=s(2+s)/(1+s)², for s≠−1. This matches option a.

after.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14059013/assets/7e5b5001794ecdf2c9b9e9102f334a63d2c59bc6f7511c2eb7fa358fc94cb0c5.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $s,$ where $x=x(s)$ and $y=y(s),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{1}{1+y},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-\frac{x}{(1+y)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{1}{1+s}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-\frac{{s}^{2}}{(1+s)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}=2s,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s} \\  & =\frac{1}{1+s}\cdot 2s-\frac{{s}^{2}}{(1+s)^{2}}\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{2s}{1+s}-\frac{{s}^{2}}{(1+s)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2s(1+s)-{s}^{2}}{(1+s)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{s(2+s)}{(1+s)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4
?

If f(x,y)=x1+y, x=s2 and y=s, compute dfds.

a
s(2+s)(1+s)2
b
s2(2+s)(1+s)
c
 s(1−s)(1+s)2
d
2+s21+s
e
1+s2(1+s)2
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y) with one independent variable s, where x=x(s) and y=y(s), can be expressed as follows:

dfds=∂f∂x⋅dxds+∂f∂y⋅dyds

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y:

∂f∂x=11+y,∂f∂y=−x(1+y)2

Writing the above results in terms of s, we get ∂f∂x=11+s,∂f∂y=−s2(1+s)2.

Next, we take the derivatives of x and y with respect to s, and we get dxds=2s,dyds=1.

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get dfds=∂f∂x⋅dxds+∂f∂y⋅dyds=11+s⋅2s−s2(1+s)2⋅1=2s1+s−s2(1+s)2=2s(1+s)−s2(1+s)2=s(2+s)(1+s)2.

verification.explanation: The chain rule gives df/ds=2s/(1+s)−s²/(1+s)²=s(2+s)/(1+s)², for s≠−1. This confirms option a and agrees with the revealed solution; the deliberately incorrect submission selected e.

\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{1}{1+y},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-\frac{x}{(1+y)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{1}{1+s}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-\frac{{s}^{2}}{(1+s)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}=2s,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14059013/assets/7e5b5001794ecdf2c9b9e9102f334a63d2c59bc6f7511c2eb7fa358fc94cb0c5.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $s,$ where $x=x(s)$ and $y=y(s),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{1}{y},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡2s}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡2s}{{sin}^{2}⁡2s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2s,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}=2\operatorname{cos}⁡2s.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s} \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡2s}\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2s)+(-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡2s}{{sin}^{2}⁡2s})\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡2s \\  & =-2-2\cdot \frac{{cos}^{2}⁡2s}{{sin}^{2}⁡2s} \\  & =-2-2{cot}^{2}⁡2s \\  & =-2{csc}^{2}⁡2s.\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡2s}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡2s}{{sin}^{2}⁡2s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2s,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}=2\operatorname{cos}⁡2s.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s} \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡2s}\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2s)+(-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡2s}{{sin}^{2}⁡2s})\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡2s \\  & =-2-2\cdot \frac{{cos}^{2}⁡2s}{{sin}^{2}⁡2s} \\  & =-2-2{cot}^{2}⁡2s \\  & =-2{csc}^{2}⁡2s.\end{aligned}
$$

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $s,$ where $x=x(s)$ and $y=y(s),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{1}{y},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡2s}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡2s}{{sin}^{2}⁡2s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2s,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}=2\operatorname{cos}⁡2s.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s} \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡2s}\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2s)+(-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡2s}{{sin}^{2}⁡2s})\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡2s \\  & =-2-2\cdot \frac{{cos}^{2}⁡2s}{{sin}^{2}⁡2s} \\  & =-2-2{cot}^{2}⁡2s \\  & =-2{csc}^{2}⁡2s.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Substituting y=x² gives f(x)=x ln(x+x²). The product and chain rules yield df/dx=ln(x+x²)+x(1+2x)/(x+x²)=ln(x+x²)+(1+2x)/(1+x), matching option b.

after.name: Question 6
after.worked_solution:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)+\frac{x}{x+y},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{x}{x+y}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+{x}^{2})+\frac{x}{x+{x}^{2}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{x}{x+{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+{x}^{2})+\frac{x}{x+{x}^{2}}+\frac{x}{x+{x}^{2}}\cdot 2x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+{x}^{2})+\frac{x+2{x}^{2}}{x+{x}^{2}} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+{x}^{2})+\frac{x(1+2x)}{x(1+x)} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+{x}^{2})+\frac{1+2x}{1+x}.\end{aligned}
$$

after.html:
Question 6
?

If f(x,y)=xln⁡(x+y) and y=x2, compute dfdx.

a
x2ln⁡(1+x)
b
ln⁡(x+x2)+1+2x1+x
c
ln⁡(1+x2)−1+3x21+2x
d
ln⁡(1+x)−1+2x21+x2
e
1+2x1+x
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y) in the case where y=y(x) can be expressed as follows: dfdx=∂f∂x+∂f∂y⋅dydx

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y: ∂f∂x=ln⁡(x+y)+xx+y,∂f∂y=xx+y

Writing the above results in terms of x, we get ∂f∂x=ln⁡(x+x2)+xx+x2,∂f∂y=xx+x2.

Next, we take the derivative y with respect to x, and we get dydx=2x.

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

dfdx=ln⁡(x+x2)+xx+x2+xx+x2⋅2x=ln⁡(x+x2)+x+2x2x+x2=ln⁡(x+x2)+x(1+2x)x(1+x)=ln⁡(x+x2)+1+2x1+x.

content.knowledge_point: Calculating the Derivative of a Multivariable Function With One Independent Variable in the Special Case
content.worked_solution:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)+\frac{x}{x+y},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{x}{x+y}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+{x}^{2})+\frac{x}{x+{x}^{2}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{x}{x+{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+{x}^{2})+\frac{x}{x+{x}^{2}}+\frac{x}{x+{x}^{2}}\cdot 2x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+{x}^{2})+\frac{x+2{x}^{2}}{x+{x}^{2}} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+{x}^{2})+\frac{x(1+2x)}{x(1+x)} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+{x}^{2})+\frac{1+2x}{1+x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 7
?

If f(x,y)=yx+1 and y=x3, compute dfdx.

a
x2(2x+3)(x+1)2
b
4x2(x−6)x+1
c
x(4x−3)x+1
d
x(3x+4)(x+1)2
e
x2(3x2−1)(x+1)2
Submit

decision.explanation: Substituting y=x³ gives f(x)=x³/(x+1). The quotient rule yields df/dx=[3x²(x+1)−x³]/(x+1)²=x²(2x+3)/(x+1)², for x≠−1. This matches option a.

after.name: Question 7
after.worked_solution:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=-\frac{y}{(x+1)^{2}},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{1}{x+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =-\frac{{x}^{3}}{(x+1)^{2}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{1}{x+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =3{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{{x}^{3}}{(x+1)^{2}}+\frac{1}{x+1}\cdot 3{x}^{2} \\  & =\frac{3{x}^{2}}{x+1}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{(x+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{3{x}^{2}(x+1)-{x}^{3}}{(x+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{3{x}^{3}+3{x}^{2}-{x}^{3}}{(x+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}(2x+3)}{(x+1)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 7

If f(x,y)=yx+1 and y=x3, compute dfdx.

a
x2(2x+3)(x+1)2
b
4x2(x−6)x+1
c
x(4x−3)x+1
d
x(3x+4)(x+1)2
e
x2(3x2−1)(x+1)2
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y) in the case where y=y(x) can be expressed as follows: dfdx=∂f∂x+∂f∂y⋅dydx

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y: ∂f∂x=−y(x+1)2,∂f∂y=1x+1

Writing the above results in terms of x, we get ∂f∂x=−x3(x+1)2,∂f∂y=1x+1.

Next, we take the derivative y with respect to x, and we get dydx=3x2.

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get dfdx=−x3(x+1)2+1x+1⋅3x2=3x2x+1−x3(x+1)2=3x2(x+1)−x3(x+1)2=3x3+3x2−x3(x+1)2=x2(2x+3)(x+1)2.

verification.explanation: The chain rule gives df/dx=−x³/(x+1)²+3x²/(x+1)=x²(2x+3)/(x+1)², for x≠−1. This agrees with the revealed solution and confirms option a. The deliberately incorrect submission selected c.

content.knowledge_point: Calculating the Derivative of a Multivariable Function With One Independent Variable in the Special Case
content.worked_solution:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=-\frac{y}{(x+1)^{2}},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{1}{x+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =-\frac{{x}^{3}}{(x+1)^{2}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{1}{x+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =3{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{{x}^{3}}{(x+1)^{2}}+\frac{1}{x+1}\cdot 3{x}^{2} \\  & =\frac{3{x}^{2}}{x+1}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{(x+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{3{x}^{2}(x+1)-{x}^{3}}{(x+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{3{x}^{3}+3{x}^{2}-{x}^{3}}{(x+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}(2x+3)}{(x+1)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 8
after.worked_solution:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}={e}^{y},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x{e}^{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & ={e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =x{e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & ={e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}+x{e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡x \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}(1+x\operatorname{cos}⁡x).\end{aligned}
$$

Question 8
?

If f(x,y)=xey and y=sin⁡x, compute dfdx.

a
esin⁡x(1+xsin⁡x)
b
esin⁡x(1+xcos⁡x)
c
ecos⁡x(1−xsin⁡x)
d
esin⁡x(1−cos⁡x)
e
ecos⁡x(1+sin⁡x)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y) in the case where y=y(x) can be expressed as follows:

dfdx=∂f∂x+∂f∂y⋅dydx

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y:

∂f∂x=ey,∂f∂y=xey

Writing the above results in terms of x, we get ∂f∂x=esin⁡x,∂f∂y=xesin⁡x.

Next, we take the derivative y with respect to x, and we get dydx=cos⁡x.

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get dfdx=esin⁡x+xesin⁡x⋅cos⁡x=esin⁡x(1+xcos⁡x).

content.knowledge_point: Calculating the Derivative of a Multivariable Function With One Independent Variable in the Special Case
content.worked_solution:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}={e}^{y},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x{e}^{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & ={e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =x{e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & ={e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}+x{e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡x \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}(1+x\operatorname{cos}⁡x).\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 9
after.worked_solution:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2}+y),\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2}+y)\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2x\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2}+{x}^{2})=2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(2{x}^{2}), \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2}+{x}^{2})=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2{x}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(2{x}^{2})+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2{x}^{2})\cdot 2x \\  & =2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(2{x}^{2})+2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(2{x}^{2}) \\  & =4x\operatorname{cos}⁡(2{x}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y) in the case where y=y(x) can be expressed as follows:

dfdx=∂f∂x+∂f∂y⋅dydx

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y:

∂f∂x=2xcos⁡(x2+y),∂f∂y=cos⁡(x2+y)

Writing the above results in terms of x, we get

∂f∂x=2xcos⁡(x2+x2)=2xcos⁡(2x2),∂f∂y=cos⁡(x2+x2)=cos⁡(2x2).

Next, we take the derivative y with respect to x, and we get

dydx=2x.

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

dfdx=2xcos⁡(2x2)+cos⁡(2x2)⋅2x=2xcos⁡(2x2)+2xcos⁡(2x2)=4xcos⁡(2x2).

\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2x\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2}+{x}^{2})=2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(2{x}^{2}), \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2}+{x}^{2})=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2{x}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(2{x}^{2})+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2{x}^{2})\cdot 2x \\  & =2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(2{x}^{2})+2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(2{x}^{2}) \\  & =4x\operatorname{cos}⁡(2{x}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

Question 10
?

If f(x,y)=1x+y and y=e−x, compute dfdx.

a
 1−e−x1+xe−x
b
 2(x+e−x)2
c
 e−x1+xe−x
d
−1+e−x(x+e−x)2
e
 1−2e−x(x+e−x)2
Submit

decision.explanation: Substituting y=e^(−x) gives f(x)=(x+e^(−x))^(−1). The chain rule yields df/dx=−(1−e^(−x))/(x+e^(−x))², matching option d.

after.name: Question 10
after.worked_solution:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=-\frac{1}{(x+y)^{2}},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-\frac{1}{(x+y)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-\frac{1}{(x+{e}^{-x})^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-{e}^{-x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{1}{(x+{e}^{-x})^{2}}-\frac{1}{(x+{e}^{-x})^{2}}\cdot (-{e}^{-x}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{(x+{e}^{-x})^{2}}+\frac{{e}^{-x}}{(x+{e}^{-x})^{2}} \\  & =\frac{-1+{e}^{-x}}{(x+{e}^{-x})^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 10
?

If f(x,y)=1x+y and y=e−x, compute dfdx.

a
 1−e−x1+xe−x
b
 2(x+e−x)2
c
 e−x1+xe−x
d
−1+e−x(x+e−x)2
e
 1−2e−x(x+e−x)2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y) in the case where y=y(x) can be expressed as follows:

dfdx=∂f∂x+∂f∂y⋅dydx

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y:

∂f∂x=−1(x+y)2,∂f∂y=−1(x+y)2

Writing the above results in terms of x, we get

∂f∂x=∂f∂y=−1(x+e−x)2.

Next, we take the derivative y with respect to x, and we get

dydx=−e−x.

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

dfdx=−1(x+e−x)2−1(x+e−x)2⋅(−e−x)=−1(x+e−x)2+e−x(x+e−x)2=−1+e−x(x+e−x)2.

content.knowledge_point: Calculating the Derivative of a Multivariable Function With One Independent Variable in the Special Case
content.worked_solution:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=-\frac{1}{(x+y)^{2}},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-\frac{1}{(x+y)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-\frac{1}{(x+{e}^{-x})^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-{e}^{-x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{1}{(x+{e}^{-x})^{2}}-\frac{1}{(x+{e}^{-x})^{2}}\cdot (-{e}^{-x}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{(x+{e}^{-x})^{2}}+\frac{{e}^{-x}}{(x+{e}^{-x})^{2}} \\  & =\frac{-1+{e}^{-x}}{(x+{e}^{-x})^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Substituting gives f(s,t)=ts e^{t+s}. Holding t constant and differentiating with respect to s gives ∂f/∂s=t e^{t+s}+ts e^{t+s}=t e^{t+s}(s+1), matching option b.

after.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14059013/assets/21cec766fe72965697304ef4288ffb2b090ddfca179210165dbcfd42ec490b27.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t)$ and $y=y(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=y{e}^{x},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}={e}^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =ts{e}^{t+s}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & ={e}^{t+s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂s} & =1, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂s} & =t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂s} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s} \\  & =(ts{e}^{t+s})(1)+({e}^{t+s})(t) \\  & =t{e}^{t+s}(s+1).\end{aligned}
$$

Let f(x,y)=yex, where x=t+s and y=ts. Calculate ∂f∂s.

a
set+s
b
tet+s(s+1)
c
et+s(s+t)
d
tet+s(s−t)
e
set+s(t+1)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y) with two independent variables s and t, where x=x(s,t) and y=y(s,t), can be expressed as follows:

∂f∂s=∂f∂x⋅∂x∂s+∂f∂y⋅∂y∂s

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y:

∂f∂x=yex,∂f∂y=ex

Writing the above results in terms of s and t, we get

∂f∂x=tset+s,∂f∂y=et+s.

Next, we take the derivatives of x and y with respect to s, and we get

∂x∂s=1,∂y∂s=t.

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

∂f∂s=∂f∂x⋅∂x∂s+∂f∂y⋅∂y∂s=(tset+s)(1)+(et+s)(t)=tet+s(s+1).

after.name: Question 12
after.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14059013/assets/21cec766fe72965697304ef4288ffb2b090ddfca179210165dbcfd42ec490b27.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t)$ and $y=y(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =-\frac{1}{({e}^{st})^{2}}=-{e}^{-2st}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-\frac{1}{({e}^{-st})^{2}}=-{e}^{2st}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂s} & =t{e}^{st}, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂s} & =-t{e}^{-st}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂s} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s} \\  & =(-{e}^{-2st})(t{e}^{st})+(-{e}^{2st})(-t{e}^{-st}) \\  & =t{e}^{st}-t{e}^{-st} \\  & =t({e}^{st}-{e}^{-st}).\end{aligned}
$$

Question 12

Let f(x,y)=1x+1y, where x=est and y=e−st. Calculate ∂f∂s.

a
2test
b
2t
c
t(e2st+e−2st)
d
2te−st
e
t(est−e−st)
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y) with two independent variables s and t, where x=x(s,t) and y=y(s,t), can be expressed as follows: ∂f∂s=∂f∂x⋅∂x∂s+∂f∂y⋅∂y∂s

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y: ∂f∂x=−1x2,∂f∂y=−1y2

Writing the above results in terms of s and t, we get ∂f∂x=−1(est)2=−e−2st,∂f∂y=−1(e−st)2=−e2st.

Next, we take the derivatives of x and y with respect to s, and we get ∂x∂s=test,∂y∂s=−te−st.

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get ∂f∂s=∂f∂x⋅∂x∂s+∂f∂y⋅∂y∂s=(−e−2st)(test)+(−e2st)(−te−st)=test−te−st=t(est−e−st).

verification.explanation: Substitution gives f(s,t)=e^(−st)+e^(st). Holding t constant yields ∂f/∂s=−t e^(−st)+t e^(st)=t(e^(st)−e^(−st)), confirming option e and the revealed solution.

Let f(x,y)=xy, where x=cos⁡t+sin⁡s and y=sin⁡t. Calculate ∂f∂t.

a
cos2⁡t−sin2⁡t+sin⁡scos⁡t
b
cos2⁡t−sin2⁡t+cos⁡scos⁡t
c
cos2⁡t−sin2⁡t+cos⁡ssin⁡t
d
1+sin⁡ssin⁡t
e
1+cos⁡scos⁡t
Submit

decision.explanation: Holding s constant, differentiate f=(cos(t)+sin(s))sin(t): ∂f/∂t=−sin²(t)+(cos(t)+sin(s))cos(t)=cos²(t)−sin²(t)+sin(s)cos(t), matching option a.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14059013/assets/118759b163a4410f66d5855d7b7b1fd9c2ee4be585e778a759997036bd95f765.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t)$ and $y=y(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡s.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂t} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂t} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂t} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t} \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡t(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡s)\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =-{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡s\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 13
?

Let f(x,y)=xy, where x=cos⁡t+sin⁡s and y=sin⁡t. Calculate ∂f∂t.

a
cos2⁡t−sin2⁡t+sin⁡scos⁡t
b
cos2⁡t−sin2⁡t+cos⁡scos⁡t
c
cos2⁡t−sin2⁡t+cos⁡ssin⁡t
d
1+sin⁡ssin⁡t
e
1+cos⁡scos⁡t
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y) with two independent variables s and t, where x=x(s,t) and y=y(s,t), can be expressed as follows: ∂f∂t=∂f∂x⋅∂x∂t+∂f∂y⋅∂y∂t

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y: ∂f∂x=y,∂f∂y=x

Writing the above results in terms of s and t, we get ∂f∂x=sin⁡t,∂f∂y=cos⁡t+sin⁡s.

Next, we take the derivatives of x and y with respect to t, and we get ∂x∂t=−sin⁡t,∂y∂t=cos⁡t.

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get ∂f∂t=∂f∂x⋅∂x∂t+∂f∂y⋅∂y∂t=sin⁡t(−sin⁡t)+(cos⁡t+sin⁡s)⋅cos⁡t=−sin2⁡t+cos2⁡t+sin⁡scos⁡t.

content.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14059013/assets/118759b163a4410f66d5855d7b7b1fd9c2ee4be585e778a759997036bd95f765.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t)$ and $y=y(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡s.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂t} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂t} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂t} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t} \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡t(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡s)\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =-{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡s\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 14
?

Let f(x,y)=xy2−2y, where x=st2 and y=s3−t. Calculate ∂f∂s.

a
7s5t2+2s3t3−6s2+4t2
b
7s6t2−8s3t3−6s2+t4
c
4s3t3−5s2+2t4
d
7s3t2−4s3t3−6s
e
3s6t2−6s2+t4
Submit

decision.explanation: Substituting gives f=st²(s³−t)²−2(s³−t)=s⁷t²−2s⁴t³+st⁴−2s³+2t. Holding t constant and differentiating gives ∂f/∂s=7s⁶t²−8s³t³−6s²+t⁴, matching option b.

after.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14059013/assets/21cec766fe72965697304ef4288ffb2b090ddfca179210165dbcfd42ec490b27.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t)$ and $y=y(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}={y}^{2},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2xy-2\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =({s}^{3}-t)^{2}={s}^{6}-2{s}^{3}t+{t}^{2}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =2(s{t}^{2})({s}^{3}-t)-2=2{s}^{4}{t}^{2}-2s{t}^{3}-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂s} & ={t}^{2}, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂s} & =3{s}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂s} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s} \\  & =({s}^{6}-2{s}^{3}t+{t}^{2})({t}^{2})+(2{s}^{4}{t}^{2}-2s{t}^{3}-2)(3{s}^{2}) \\  & ={s}^{6}{t}^{2}-2{s}^{3}{t}^{3}+{t}^{4}+6{s}^{6}{t}^{2}-6{s}^{3}{t}^{3}-6{s}^{2} \\  & =7{s}^{6}{t}^{2}-8{s}^{3}{t}^{3}-6{s}^{2}+{t}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 14

Let f(x,y)=xy2−2y, where x=st2 and y=s3−t. Calculate ∂f∂s.

a
7s5t2+2s3t3−6s2+4t2
b
7s6t2−8s3t3−6s2+t4
c
4s3t3−5s2+2t4
d
7s3t2−4s3t3−6s
e
3s6t2−6s2+t4
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y) with two independent variables s and t, where x=x(s,t) and y=y(s,t), can be expressed as follows: ∂f∂s=∂f∂x⋅∂x∂s+∂f∂y⋅∂y∂s

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y: ∂f∂x=y2,∂f∂y=2xy−2

Writing the above results in terms of s and t, we get ∂f∂x=(s3−t)2=s6−2s3t+t2,∂f∂y=2(st2)(s3−t)−2=2s4t2−2st3−2.

Next, we take the derivatives of x and y with respect to s, and we get ∂x∂s=t2,∂y∂s=3s2.

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get ∂f∂s=∂f∂x⋅∂x∂s+∂f∂y⋅∂y∂s=(s6−2s3t+t2)(t2)+(2s4t2−2st3−2)(3s2)=s6t2−2s3t3+t4+6s6t2−6s3t3−6s2=7s6t2−8s3t3−6s2+t4.

verification.explanation: Holding t constant, the chain rule gives ∂f/∂s=t²(s³−t)²+3s²[2st²(s³−t)−2]=7s⁶t²−8s³t³−6s²+t⁴. This confirms option b and agrees with the revealed solution.

content.knowledge_point: Calculating the Derivative of a Multivariable Function With Two Independent Variables
content.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14059013/assets/21cec766fe72965697304ef4288ffb2b090ddfca179210165dbcfd42ec490b27.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t)$ and $y=y(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}={y}^{2},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2xy-2\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =({s}^{3}-t)^{2}={s}^{6}-2{s}^{3}t+{t}^{2}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =2(s{t}^{2})({s}^{3}-t)-2=2{s}^{4}{t}^{2}-2s{t}^{3}-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂s} & ={t}^{2}, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂s} & =3{s}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂s} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s} \\  & =({s}^{6}-2{s}^{3}t+{t}^{2})({t}^{2})+(2{s}^{4}{t}^{2}-2s{t}^{3}-2)(3{s}^{2}) \\  & ={s}^{6}{t}^{2}-2{s}^{3}{t}^{3}+{t}^{4}+6{s}^{6}{t}^{2}-6{s}^{3}{t}^{3}-6{s}^{2} \\  & =7{s}^{6}{t}^{2}-8{s}^{3}{t}^{3}-6{s}^{2}+{t}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14059013/assets/118759b163a4410f66d5855d7b7b1fd9c2ee4be585e778a759997036bd95f765.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t)$ and $y=y(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2+y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2+t{e}^{s}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =s{e}^{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂t} & =0, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂t} & ={e}^{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂t} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t} \\  & =(2+t{e}^{s})(0)+(s{e}^{s})({e}^{s}) \\  & =s{e}^{2s}.\end{aligned}

Question 15

Let f(x,y)=2x+xy, where x=ses and y=tes. Calculate ∂f∂t.

a
sest
b
stes
c
se2s
d
test
e
te2s
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y) with two independent variables s and t, where x=x(s,t) and y=y(s,t), can be expressed as follows: ∂f∂t=∂f∂x⋅∂x∂t+∂f∂y⋅∂y∂t

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y: ∂f∂x=2+y,∂f∂y=x

Writing the above results in terms of s and t, we get ∂f∂x=2+tes,∂f∂y=ses.

Next, we take the derivatives of x and y with respect to t, and we get ∂x∂t=0,∂y∂t=es.

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get ∂f∂t=∂f∂x⋅∂x∂t+∂f∂y⋅∂y∂t=(2+tes)(0)+(ses)(es)=se2s.

content.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14059013/assets/118759b163a4410f66d5855d7b7b1fd9c2ee4be585e778a759997036bd95f765.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t)$ and $y=y(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2+y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2+t{e}^{s}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =s{e}^{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂t} & =0, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂t} & ={e}^{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂t} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t} \\  & =(2+t{e}^{s})(0)+(s{e}^{s})({e}^{s}) \\  & =s{e}^{2s}.\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14059013/assets/be6afcdd0ad9ae0d7ef377c4918442a64e1186c90c25e27ec6c224d816a602fd.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y,z)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t),y=y(s,t)$ and $z=z(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x,y$ and $z:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{1}{x},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-2{e}^{y},\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=4.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{1}{t{s}^{2}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-2{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡({t}^{2}+{s}^{2})}=-2({t}^{2}+{s}^{2}), \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂s} & =2ts, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂s} & =\frac{2s}{{t}^{2}+{s}^{2}}, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂s} & =2s.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂s} & =(\frac{1}{t{s}^{2}})\cdot 2ts+(-2({t}^{2}+{s}^{2}))\cdot (\frac{2s}{{t}^{2}+{s}^{2}})+(4)\cdot 2s \\  & =\frac{2}{s}-4s+8s \\  & =\frac{2}{s}+4s \\  & =\frac{2(1+2{s}^{2})}{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 16

Let f(x,y,z)=ln⁡x−2ey+4z, where x=ts2, y=ln⁡(t2+s2) and z=s2. Calculate ∂f∂s.

a
1+t2s
b
2(1+2s2)s
c
st+12
d
st(s2t2+1)
e
t2−s2s
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y,z) with two independent variables s and t, where x=x(s,t),y=y(s,t) and z=z(s,t), can be expressed as follows: ∂f∂s=∂f∂x⋅∂x∂s+∂f∂y⋅∂y∂s+∂f∂z⋅∂z∂s

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x,y and z: ∂f∂x=1x,∂f∂y=−2ey,∂f∂z=4.

Writing the above results in terms of s and t, we get ∂f∂x=1ts2,∂f∂y=−2eln⁡(t2+s2)=−2(t2+s2),∂f∂z=4.

Next, we take the derivatives of x, y, and z with respect to s, and we get ∂x∂s=2ts,∂y∂s=2st2+s2,∂z∂s=2s.

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get ∂f∂s=(1ts2)⋅2ts+(−2(t2+s2))⋅(2st2+s2)+(4)⋅2s=2s−4s+8s=2s+4s=2(1+2s2)s.

content.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14059013/assets/be6afcdd0ad9ae0d7ef377c4918442a64e1186c90c25e27ec6c224d816a602fd.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y,z)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t),y=y(s,t)$ and $z=z(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x,y$ and $z:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{1}{x},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-2{e}^{y},\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=4.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{1}{t{s}^{2}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-2{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡({t}^{2}+{s}^{2})}=-2({t}^{2}+{s}^{2}), \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂s} & =2ts, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂s} & =\frac{2s}{{t}^{2}+{s}^{2}}, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂s} & =2s.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂s} & =(\frac{1}{t{s}^{2}})\cdot 2ts+(-2({t}^{2}+{s}^{2}))\cdot (\frac{2s}{{t}^{2}+{s}^{2}})+(4)\cdot 2s \\  & =\frac{2}{s}-4s+8s \\  & =\frac{2}{s}+4s \\  & =\frac{2(1+2{s}^{2})}{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14059013/assets/b593a1b60fe8c1aef2c5c229ff426db350e6296b9ecb767494283f0fa3342072.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y,z)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t),y=y(s,t)$ and $z=z(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x,y$ and $z:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=yz,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=xz,\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=xy.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =ts{e}^{t+s}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =2t{e}^{s}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =2s{e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂t} & =0, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂t} & =s{e}^{t}, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂t} & ={e}^{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂t} & =(ts{e}^{t+s})\cdot 0+(2t{e}^{s})\cdot s{e}^{t}+(2s{e}^{t})\cdot {e}^{s} \\  & =2ts{e}^{t+s}+2s{e}^{t+s} \\  & =2s(t+1){e}^{t+s}.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y,z) with two independent variables s and t, where x=x(s,t),y=y(s,t) and z=z(s,t), can be expressed as follows: ∂f∂t=∂f∂x⋅∂x∂t+∂f∂y⋅∂y∂t+∂f∂z⋅∂z∂t

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x,y and z: ∂f∂x=yz,∂f∂y=xz,∂f∂z=xy.

Writing the above results in terms of s and t, we get ∂f∂x=tset+s,∂f∂y=2tes,∂f∂z=2set.

Next, we take the derivatives of x, y, and z with respect to t, and we get ∂x∂t=0,∂y∂t=set,∂z∂t=es.

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

∂f∂t=(tset+s)⋅0+(2tes)⋅set+(2set)⋅es=2tset+s+2set+s=2s(t+1)et+s.

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y,z)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t),y=y(s,t)$ and $z=z(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x,y$ and $z:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=yz,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=xz,\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=xy.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =ts{e}^{t+s}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =2t{e}^{s}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =2s{e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂t} & =0, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂t} & =s{e}^{t}, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂t} & ={e}^{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂t} & =(ts{e}^{t+s})\cdot 0+(2t{e}^{s})\cdot s{e}^{t}+(2s{e}^{t})\cdot {e}^{s} \\  & =2ts{e}^{t+s}+2s{e}^{t+s} \\  & =2s(t+1){e}^{t+s}.\end{aligned}
$$

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y,z) with two independent variables s and t, where x=x(s,t),y=y(s,t) and z=z(s,t), can be expressed as follows: ∂f∂t=∂f∂x⋅∂x∂t+∂f∂y⋅∂y∂t+∂f∂z⋅∂z∂t

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x,y and z: ∂f∂x=yz,∂f∂y=xz,∂f∂z=xy.

Writing the above results in terms of s and t, we get ∂f∂x=tset+s,∂f∂y=2tes,∂f∂z=2set.

Next, we take the derivatives of x, y, and z with respect to t, and we get ∂x∂t=0,∂y∂t=set,∂z∂t=es.

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

∂f∂t=(tset+s)⋅0+(2tes)⋅set+(2set)⋅es=2tset+s+2set+s=2s(t+1)et+s.

Your Answer:
2t(s+1)et+s

Let f(x,y,z)=3x−2y+z, where x=s+t, y=s2−t2 and z=s. Calculate ∂f∂t.

a
4t+3
b
2t−s−3
c
8t−s
d
5t+4s−1
e
2s−1

decision.explanation: Holding s constant, ∂x/∂t=1, ∂y/∂t=−2t, and ∂z/∂t=0. Thus ∂f/∂t=3(1)−2(−2t)+0=4t+3, matching option a.

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂t} & =(3)\cdot 1+(-2)\cdot (-2t)+(1)\cdot 0 \\  & =4t+3.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 18

Let f(x,y,z)=3x−2y+z, where x=s+t, y=s2−t2 and z=s. Calculate ∂f∂t.

a
4t+3
b
2t−s−3
c
8t−s
d
5t+4s−1
e
2s−1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y,z) with two independent variables s and t, where x=x(s,t),y=y(s,t) and z=z(s,t), can be expressed as follows: ∂f∂t=∂f∂x⋅∂x∂t+∂f∂y⋅∂y∂t+∂f∂z⋅∂z∂t.

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x,y and z: ∂f∂x=3,∂f∂y=−2,∂f∂z=1.

Next, we take the derivatives of x, y, and z with respect to t, and we get ∂x∂t=1,∂y∂t=−2t,∂z∂t=0.

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

∂f∂t=(3)⋅1+(−2)⋅(−2t)+(1)⋅0=4t+3.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14059013/assets/be6afcdd0ad9ae0d7ef377c4918442a64e1186c90c25e27ec6c224d816a602fd.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y,z)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t),y=y(s,t)$ and $z=z(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x,y$ and $z:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=4,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=3,\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂s} & =4s, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂s} & =1, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂s} & =8s.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂s} & =(4)\cdot 4s+(3)\cdot 1+(-2)\cdot 8s \\  & =16s+3-16s \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Substituting gives f=(s²+t²)/(s+t). Holding s constant, ∂f/∂t=[2t(s+t)−(s²+t²)]/(s+t)²=(−s²+2st+t²)/(s+t)². Thus c₁=−1, c₂=2, c₃=1, and their sum is 2.

after.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14059013/assets/b593a1b60fe8c1aef2c5c229ff426db350e6296b9ecb767494283f0fa3342072.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y,z)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t),y=y(s,t)$ and $z=z(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x,y$ and $z:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=-\frac{y+z}{{x}^{2}},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{1}{x},\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=\frac{1}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =-\frac{{s}^{2}+{t}^{2}}{(s+t)^{2}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{1}{s+t}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{1}{s+t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂t} & =1, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂t} & =0, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂t} & =2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂t} & =-\frac{{s}^{2}+{t}^{2}}{(s+t)^{2}}\cdot (1)+\frac{1}{s+t}\cdot 0+\frac{1}{s+t}\cdot 2t \\  & =\frac{-({s}^{2}+{t}^{2})+2t(s+t)}{(s+t)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{t}^{2}+2ts-{s}^{2}}{(s+t)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, ${c}_{1}=-1,$ ${c}_{2}=2$ and ${c}_{3}=1,$ and therefore

$$
{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}+{c}_{3}=-1+2+1=2.
$$

a
1
b
−2
c
0
d
2
e

Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y,z) with two independent variables s and t, where x=x(s,t),y=y(s,t) and z=z(s,t), can be expressed as follows: ∂f∂t=∂f∂x⋅∂x∂t+∂f∂y⋅∂y∂t+∂f∂z⋅∂z∂t

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x,y and z: ∂f∂x=−y+zx2,∂f∂y=1x,∂f∂z=1x.

Writing the above results in terms of s and t, we get

∂f∂x=−s2+t2(s+t)2,∂f∂y=1s+t,∂f∂z=1s+t.

Next, we take the derivatives of x, y, and z with respect to t, and we get ∂x∂t=1,∂y∂t=0,∂z∂t=2t.

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get ∂f∂t=−s2+t2(s+t)2⋅(1)+1s+t⋅0+1s+t⋅2t=−(s2+t2)+2t(s+t)(s+t)2=t2+2ts−s2(s+t)2.

Finally, c1=−1, c2=2 and c3=1, and therefore c1+c2+c3=−1+2+1=2.

content.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14059013/assets/b593a1b60fe8c1aef2c5c229ff426db350e6296b9ecb767494283f0fa3342072.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y,z)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t),y=y(s,t)$ and $z=z(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x,y$ and $z:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=-\frac{y+z}{{x}^{2}},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{1}{x},\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=\frac{1}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =-\frac{{s}^{2}+{t}^{2}}{(s+t)^{2}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{1}{s+t}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{1}{s+t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂t} & =1, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂t} & =0, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂t} & =2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂t} & =-\frac{{s}^{2}+{t}^{2}}{(s+t)^{2}}\cdot (1)+\frac{1}{s+t}\cdot 0+\frac{1}{s+t}\cdot 2t \\  & =\frac{-({s}^{2}+{t}^{2})+2t(s+t)}{(s+t)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{t}^{2}+2ts-{s}^{2}}{(s+t)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, ${c}_{1}=-1,$ ${c}_{2}=2$ and ${c}_{3}=1,$ and therefore

$$
{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}+{c}_{3}=-1+2+1=2.
$$

history.html:
The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y,z) with two independent variables s and t, where x=x(s,t),y=y(s,t) and z=z(s,t), can be expressed as follows: ∂f∂t=∂f∂x⋅∂x∂t+∂f∂y⋅∂y∂t+∂f∂z⋅∂z∂t

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x,y and z: ∂f∂x=−y+zx2,∂f∂y=1x,∂f∂z=1x.

Writing the above results in terms of s and t, we get

∂f∂x=−s2+t2(s+t)2,∂f∂y=1s+t,∂f∂z=1s+t.

Next, we take the derivatives of x, y, and z with respect to t, and we get ∂x∂t=1,∂y∂t=0,∂z∂t=2t.

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get ∂f∂t=−s2+t2(s+t)2⋅(1)+1s+t⋅0+1s+t⋅2t=−(s2+t2)+2t(s+t)(s+t)2=t2+2ts−s2(s+t)2.

Finally, c1=−1, c2=2 and c3=1, and therefore c1+c2+c3=−1+2+1=2.
